column1: # Narration for the projects demo: <caption><TAB><what Kokoro says>. Captions must match the demo script's caption: steps.

column2: This is Flotilla. It runs coding agents in their own cloud VMs, one thread per task. Now it has projects: GitHub repos it keeps ready, so every new thread starts on its own branch in seconds.
Flotilla talks to GitHub through the g h command line tool you're already signed in with, so there's nothing new to set up.
Add project lists the repos your account can see. I'll pick the playground, a tiny TypeScript library.
This repo has a dot agents setup script, so Flotilla runs it in every setup. Scripts added here would run just before it.

column1: Setup runs once, threads copy it
column2: Flotilla now prepares a VM for the project. It clones the repo and runs setup, and every new thread will start from a copy of that VM.
Done. From now on, Flotilla checks main every minute, and prepares each new commit in the background.
Now, a new thread. The project is picked, and the branch picker says new branch, from the latest main.
I'll ask Haiku, a small, cheap model, to add jitter to the retry backoff, and to open a draft pull request.
The thread copies the prepared VM, switches to its own branch, and reruns setup, which takes seconds when nothing changed. Then the agent gets the prompt.

column1: The agent works in its own VM
column2: The agent works in its own VM, and Flotilla follows along.
The agent pushed its branch and opened a draft pull request. The header shows the repo, the branch, and the commit it started from. Below it, the pull request and its checks.
Meanwhile, a teammate changed the same line on main. The header says the branch is one commit behind, and the pull request now has a conflict.
Resolve, like Fix for failing checks, writes a prompt for the agent and puts it in the composer, so I can read it first. Nothing is sent until I press send.
The agent merged main, kept both the cap and the jitter, and pushed. The checks are green.
Ready for review takes it out of draft. Merge uses the repo's own merge method, after a confirmation.
Merged. Flotilla sees it straight away and prepares the new main, so the next thread starts from it.
Now someone pushes a commit that breaks setup. The setup run fails, and new threads keep starting from the last good one.
Fix in a new thread opens a thread with the commit, the failing script, its exit code, and the end of its log. I'll send it.

column1: Threads start even when setup fails
column2: A thread starts even when setup fails, so the agent can fix it.

column1: Start on a branch or pull request
column2: New threads can also start on an existing branch, or an open pull request. Search for it, or paste a link.
And any project thread can hand its branch to a fresh thread, from its menu.
In settings: a prefix for new branches, and how soon idle VMs stop, so threads cost nothing while you're away.
That's projects in Flotilla. Repos kept ready, a branch for every thread, and pull requests you can fix and merge without leaving the app.
